turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Nice to meet you too, Dr. Smith. I appreciate you taking the time. Well, I suppose the short version—or, well, probably the long version, if I'm being completely honest with myself—is that things have just gotten completely overwhelming lately. I'm a software developer, and I've always had a lot on my plate, which I used to think I could handle because, you know, I got through my graduate program and I’ve been in this industry a long time, so I should know how to manage a project. 

But what finally pushed me to actually make this appointment and come in today is that I just... I can’t seem to organize the moving parts anymore. There are just so many of them, and it feels like they're all spinning out of control. I've got all these complex patent notes I need to review and synthesize, I'm trying to handle workshop prep for my department, there are gallery deadlines I'm somehow supposed to keep track of on the side, and then there's the day-to-day team decisions at work that constantly need my input. It's just an absolute mountain of information. 

And the real problem is, I look at all of it and I just can't sort it out or put it in any logical sequence. Instead of sitting down, making a plan, and figuring out what's most critical, I just end up starting whatever is loudest. You know what I mean? Like, whatever email just dinged, or whoever is messaging me right that second, rather than what actually matters or what's going to move the needle on my main projects. I'll spend ten hours working, completely exhausted, and realize I entirely ignored the core deliverables because I was just reacting to whatever grabbed my attention first. It's incredibly frustrating, and I just feel like I'm constantly failing to prioritize because I can't put all these different pieces in order in my head.

symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient explicitly states they cannot organize the moving parts of their work, cannot sort tasks into a logical sequence, and fail to prioritize or make a plan.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes being easily diverted by extraneous stimuli, such as dinging emails or incoming messages, reacting to whatever grabs their attention first rather than focusing on core tasks.

turns.doctor_question: Looking back at your childhood and throughout your school years, did you find that you struggled with this kind of organization and prioritization, or is this something that has only become a problem for you more recently?
turns.patient_response:
Well, you know, it's funny you ask that, because for a long time I thought this was just a recent thing. I mean, the workload now is so heavy, I figured anyone would struggle, right? But... when I really sit down and think about it, and look back at how things used to be... no, it's definitely not new. It's just that the stakes are higher now. 

If I really think back to grade school—and I'm talking way back, like third or fourth grade, long before I was even a teenager—it was always there. I remember my mom keeping all my old report cards in this big cedar chest, and if you look at them, the comments from the teachers were almost identical every single year. They’d always write something like, "He's a very bright boy, but he spends half the day daydreaming out the window." Or they'd say I wasn't living up to my potential because I couldn't keep track of anything. 

And the homework... oh man, the homework. It wasn't that I didn't do it. I'd sit at the kitchen table, do the math worksheets, write the spelling sentences, put it all in my folder... and then the next day, the teacher would ask for it, and it was just gone. I’d lose the whole homework folder somewhere between my house and my desk at school. Or I'd actually have it in my backpack, but when it came time to hand it in, I’d just completely forget to take it out and put it in the tray. I'd find finished assignments crammed at the bottom of my bag three weeks later, all crumpled up. So, yeah, I guess the inability to keep things organized and actually follow through on the sequence of steps... that’s been happening for a very, very long time. It just looked like lost folders back then instead of missed project deliverables.

symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient describes an inability to follow through on the sequence of steps and failing to complete the process of turning in schoolwork.
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient explicitly confirms a long-standing inability to keep things organized and track of their work.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient recalls frequently losing their entire homework folder between their house and their desk at school.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient mentions that teachers frequently commented on them spending half the day daydreaming out the window.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient describes forgetting to take finished assignments out of their backpack to hand them in.

turns.doctor_question: Looking back at your younger years, did you often feel like you were driven by a motor, or did you have a hard time staying seated when you were expected to?
turns.patient_response:
No, not really. I mean, I know what you're talking about—like the kids who were always bouncing off the walls or getting in trouble for running around the classroom when they were supposed to be doing silent reading. But that wasn't me at all. In fact, it was almost the opposite. 

I was always pretty quiet, you know? Like I said about the report cards, the teachers were always saying I was daydreaming, not that I was disruptive. I'd just sit there at my desk, completely still, but my mind would be a million miles away. I'd be looking at a spot on the chalkboard or out the window at the playground, and I wouldn't even realize the teacher had moved on to a completely different subject. I didn't feel this urge to get up and run around, and I never felt restless in my body, like I had some kind of motor running inside me. It was more like... well, like my brain was just floating away from wherever my body was sitting. 

I remember in fifth grade, Mr. Henderson's class, we had these assigned seats in rows, and I was in the third row, second seat back. He was a real stickler for posture and staying seated, and I never got in trouble for fidgeting or getting out of my chair. But I did get in trouble because he'd call on me to read the next paragraph in our history book, and I wouldn't even know what page we were on. I was perfectly happy just sitting there, not moving a muscle, completely lost in my own thoughts about whatever sci-fi book I was reading at home or trying to figure out how a clock worked. So, no, the physical restlessness, the hyperactive stuff... I never really dealt with that. It was always just the mental drift.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes their mind being 'a million miles away' and getting 'completely lost in my own thoughts,' indicating distractibility by unrelated thoughts.
symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient explicitly states they 'never got in trouble for fidgeting' and would sit 'completely still.'
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient denies having a hard time staying seated, stating they 'never got in trouble for... getting out of my chair.'
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient explicitly denies physical restlessness, stating they 'never felt restless in my body' and 'didn't feel this urge to get up and run around.'
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient explicitly denies feeling 'like I had some kind of motor running inside me.'

turns.doctor_question: In your current adult life, do you find yourself frequently interrupting others when they are speaking or struggling to wait your turn in conversations?
turns.patient_response:
No, I wouldn't say that's a problem for me. I mean, I know how annoying it is when people do that—there's this one guy on our daily stand-up calls, Dave, who just completely steamrolls everyone. You'll be in the middle of explaining why a particular sprint is delayed because of a dependency issue with the API, and he just jumps right in with his own tangent about something entirely unrelated. It drives the whole team crazy, and I'm always very conscious of not wanting to be that guy. 

So, no, I don't really interrupt people. If anything, I probably wait too long to speak up. Because I'm usually trying to process what they're saying, or honestly, because I've drifted off a bit and I'm trying to piece together the context clues of the conversation so I don't sound foolish when I finally do chime in. Like, if we're in a meeting about the new user interface, I'll let everyone else talk, and I'll just sit there nodding, trying to make sure I haven't missed a crucial detail while my brain was off thinking about a block of code from yesterday. 

And as for waiting my turn... I'm perfectly fine waiting. Sometimes I prefer it, actually. It gives me a minute to try and gather my thoughts, even if those thoughts are a bit scattered. I'm definitely not the type to blurt things out or talk over someone. I just... I let them finish, and sometimes by the time they do, I've forgotten what I was going to say anyway, so it just resolves itself, I guess. But yeah, interrupting or being impatient in conversations isn't really something I struggle with.

symptom_reasoning.S003: The patient admits to drifting off during conversations and having to piece together context clues because they weren't fully listening.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes being distracted by unrelated thoughts, such as thinking about a block of code from yesterday during a meeting.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient explicitly states they are not the type to blurt things out.
symptom_reasoning.S017: The patient explicitly denies having trouble waiting their turn, stating they are perfectly fine waiting.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient explicitly denies interrupting people or talking over someone.
